summary.text: 唱 is a phonosemantic character: 口 marks the speaking or singing domain, while 昌 supplies a sound cue. Early lexicographic evidence glosses it as “lead/guide”; later reported uses include singing, calling out, and a song or tune, though their chronology is not established. [ref002][ref003][ref013][ref015][ref026]

formation.text: The traditional analysis is phonosemantic: 口 contributes the semantic category and 昌 is phonetic. The evidence supports this analysis but does not establish the earliest surviving form or a dated sequence for 唱. [ref002][ref003][ref014][ref023]

components.text: 口 is the semantic component, marking the character's association with vocal activity. No separate earlier form for 口 as used here is established. [ref002][ref003][ref023]

昌 supplies the sound cue in the traditional analysis. Zhengzhang reconstructions give 昌 *tʰjaŋ and 唱 *tʰjaŋs; these system-specific forms suggest a relationship, while other reported reconstructions differ. [ref019][ref020][ref029][ref031]

sound.text: In Zhengzhang's Old Chinese reconstruction, 昌 *tʰjaŋ is compared with 唱 *tʰjaŋs. The forms are related in this system; they are reconstructions, not directly recorded ancient pronunciations. [ref019]

Middle Chinese categories report related initials and rhyme categories for 昌 and 唱, but different tones; this is compatible with a sound cue, without documenting their pronunciation at formation. [ref027][ref029]
sound.component_reading: initial 昌, level tone, 陽 rhyme, open division III (Guangyun fanqie 尺良)
sound.character_reading: initial 昌, departing tone, 漾 rhyme, open division III (Guangyun fanqie 尺亮)

history.text: The traditional account analyzes 唱 as 口 plus phonetic 昌 and gives its meaning as “lead/guide.” A Small Seal form is reported, but no inspected evidence establishes the earliest surviving form or a graphic sequence. [ref003][ref013][ref014][ref023][ref025]
Older texts are reported to have often used 倡 for 唱. 倡 is a related graph analyzed with 人 and phonetic 昌; the evidence does not establish it as an earlier graphic form of 唱. [ref013][ref017]

The phonetic analysis has a plausible Zhengzhang Old Chinese comparison, but another reported reconstruction differs; the detailed sound history therefore remains unsettled. Modern Mandarin and Cantonese readings alone do not prove the ancient sound relation. [ref019][ref020][ref021][ref031]

uncertainties.text: The evidence does not establish a dated sequence of graphic changes, corruption, or reanalysis within 唱. The reported seal-style image is a modern redraw, not an inspected artifact image. [ref023][ref025][ref033][ref036]
The cited sense examples support several reported uses, but were not independently checked against dated witnesses; their order does not establish a semantic pathway. [ref015][ref026]
The proposed Sino-Tibetan comparisons concern the spoken word and remain unverified; they do not establish the graphic origin of the character. [ref022]

senses.text: The traditional lexicographic gloss is “lead/guide”; a cited passage describes the yu leading while other instruments follow. This supports an early reported sense, but the surviving written form's date is unresolved. [ref003][ref013][ref024]
Singing and chanting are reported uses. The evidence does not securely date them relative to the “lead” sense. [ref007][ref015][ref026]
Calling or shouting is reported in cited examples, but their chronology and relation to the other senses are not established here. [ref015][ref026]
The character is also reported with the noun sense “song” or “tune.” The evidence does not establish when this sense developed. [ref007][ref015][ref026]

limitations.text: The reported senses are not connected into a sequence because the cited examples do not establish the chronology or semantic transitions. [ref015][ref026]

overview.text: 唱 combines 口, marking vocal activity, with 昌 as a sound cue. Its early gloss is “lead/guide”; singing, calling out, and song or tune are also reported senses, without a demonstrated order. [ref002][ref003][ref015][ref026]

components.text: 口 marks the vocal domain of the character. [ref002][ref003]
昌 is analyzed as the sound cue; historical reconstructions support a plausible comparison, though systems differ. [ref019][ref020][ref031]

relationships.text: The traditional analysis identifies 口 as the semantic component of 唱. [ref002][ref003]
The traditional analysis assigns 昌 the phonetic role; historical sound comparisons are plausible but reconstruction-system dependent. [ref003][ref019][ref020][ref031]
